title: Fed’s Barkin Signals Hope: Inflation Could Drop “In Short Order,” He Says】
body:
Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Thomas Barkin told policymakers on Tuesday that he believes inflation could start easing “in short order,” even as the central bank grapples with lingering price pressures tied to global geopolitical tensions. Barkin’s remarks, delivered during a regional banking conference, signal a cautiously optimistic shift among some Fed officials who have been wrestling with the prospect that the disinflationary process may be slower than initially hoped.

Barkin emphasized that while the trajectory of consumer prices appears to be turning downward, the outlook remains clouded by external factors, notably the ongoing conflict in Iran. “I’m open to the possibility that inflation could come back down in short order, but we have to stay mindful that elevated prices could persist because of the war’s impact on energy and commodities,” he said. His comments reflect a broader debate within the Fed about how to balance the need for continued monetary tightening with the risk of choking off an already fragile recovery.

The Richmond president’s optimism contrasts with the more guarded tone of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, who has repeatedly warned that the path to price stability is “uneven” and that policy decisions must be data‑driven. Barkin’s assessment, however, aligns with a growing segment of the Fed’s voting members who see recent declines in headline CPI and core inflation as early signs that the aggressive rate hikes of the past year are beginning to work. If the trend holds, the central bank could consider pausing further increases or even modestly easing policy later this year, a move that would be welcomed by markets still jittery over the prospect of a prolonged tightening cycle.

Analysts note that the Iranian conflict adds a layer of uncertainty that could complicate any near‑term improvement in inflation. The war has already pushed crude oil prices higher, and sanctions on Iranian oil exports have tightened global supply. Higher energy costs tend to ripple through transportation, manufacturing, and household expenses, potentially offsetting gains made in other price categories. Moreover, supply‑chain disruptions linked to the conflict could linger, keeping input costs elevated for months. “Even if domestic demand cools, external shocks can keep headline inflation stubbornly high,” said Maria Torres, senior economist at Global Insights.

Barkin also warned that the Fed must remain vigilant about the labor market’s resilience, which continues to support wage growth. Strong employment figures have historically fed into inflationary pressures, as higher wages translate into increased consumer spending. While the unemployment rate remains near historic lows, some economists see early signs of softening in job openings and hiring rates. If labor market momentum begins to wane, it could reinforce the inflation‑decline narrative that Barkin is hinting at.

The Richmond president’s comments arrive at a pivotal moment for the Fed’s policy calendar. With the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting slated for early November, policymakers will assess fresh data on consumer prices, core services, and global energy markets. Should inflation indeed show a sustained downward trend, the Fed may opt for a more dovish stance, potentially pausing rate hikes for the first time since early 2022. Conversely, any resurgence of price pressures—particularly from oil or food—could compel the central bank to resume a more aggressive tightening path.

Looking ahead, the Fed’s ability to navigate the delicate balance between curbing inflation and sustaining economic growth will hinge on how quickly external shocks subside and whether domestic demand continues to moderate. Barkin’s tentative optimism offers a glimpse of a possible turning point, but the road to price stability remains fraught with geopolitical and market uncertainties. As the central bank gathers more evidence in the coming weeks, its next moves will shape expectations for interest rates, credit conditions, and the broader trajectory of the U.S. economy.
